trans-unit.source: Plan, record, organize and share your trails.
Your hiking companion and GPS track manager. Open to all your outdoor activities.
No account required — try it right away.

Record your track, follow an existing trail, and stay on course with directions and live stats (elevation gain, distance, time remaining). Take photos that attach directly to the trail. Offline maps and printing included.
Group your trails into collections, add tags, sort and filter to find anything. Edit, compare, and manage your library however you like.
Detailed elevation profile, trail description, waypoints, estimated walking time, breaks, path waymarking, path characteristics. Plan your outing in advance — and review it when you get back.
Attach your photos and find them again on the map. Share your trails with friends or the community, import and export as GPX, print for your outing.
One app for everything you do outdoors — from scouting the map to reliving the outing.
Your trails, your tracks, your data.

Auditable code under the Apache-2.0 license. Nothing is hidden: you can check it and contribute. Trailence will always be free and open source — no 'premium' accounts. An open trail database that anyone can help grow.
No ads, no trackers, nothing to resell. We don't live off your data — we protect it. And it stays yours: export it or delete everything, anytime.
One account, with your trails synced across Web and Android. Find them on every device, wherever you are.
An open, documented, quality trail database — a work in progress.
No locked-down copyright, no empty listings: real trails, documented and verified. It starts small and grows with you — help us build the first truly open trail database.
Create a free account to find your tracks on all your devices — Web and Android.
Your email is used only to confirm your sign-up and reset your password. No newsletters, ever, and never shared with third parties.

Minimum distance between each recorded point

If the value is too low, the track quality may decrease due to GPS imprecision.
A value that is too high also leads to a low-quality track with long straight lines.
Additionally, shorter distances result in more recorded points, which can increase battery consumption.
We recommend setting the value between 5 and 15 meters (approximately 16 to 50 feet) for a good balance.
Minimum time between each recorded point

If you want to limit the number of recorded points, in order to reduce battery consumption, you can use a longer minimum time between each point.
The minimum distance between each point is also taken into account, so both the minimum distance and the minimum time must be reached before recording a new point.
We recommend a value between 2 and 5 seconds.

The altitude recorded by the GPS often shows a discrepancy compared to reality.
Here, you can adjust it by specifying a correction value.
For example, if your GPS is always about {{1}} {{2}} higher than the real altitude, you can enter -{{1}}.
Since every device is different, the configuration is done per device.
Number of days a downloaded map is valid
When you download a map to make it available offline, this setting defines how long it will be retained. It also prevents re-downloading a map if it was recently downloaded, saving time.
When you add a photo larger than the maximum size, it will be automatically resized.

Photos are automatically converted to JPEG format, and this setting determines the compression quality. 100% provides maximum quality with low compression. We recommend 90%, which maintains very good quality while still allowing good compression.

When you store a photo, the maximum pixel size and quality are applied. If the result is a file size larger than this value, the size and quality will be slightly reduced until the file size is below this threshold.

When a photo is displayed, it is downloaded and then cached on your device. This avoids having to download a photo each time, and therefore makes the display faster. It also allows you to view photos offline. So, if you plan to follow a trail that contains photos, and you want to be able to view the photos offline during your hike, by viewing the photos before you start the hike while you have network access, they will be available offline.
You can add maps from thunderforest.com if you have an account on their web site (a free account is available). Enter your API key below
This speed is used to estimate the hike duration. It is weighted according to the elevation and duration. By default the value is 3.1 mi/h (5 km/h), which corresponds to the average speed of a hiker.

When displaying a hike's duration, we distinguish short stops (to take a break, admire the view, etc.) and long stops (like a picnic).

Short stops are included in the total duration, as it's normal to have brief pauses. However, when a long stop is detected, its duration is deducted from the hike time so the time shown doesn't depend on how long you took a nap 😉. The deducted time appears in the Breaks section.

To detect long stops, you can configure two parameters: a perimeter and a minimum duration. A stop is considered long when you stay within this perimeter for at least the set minimum time.

A live tracking group lets you share your location during an activity.
Anyone can join a group using a link or a QR code, without necessarily needing a Trailence account.
Each member’s location is regularly recorded and shared with the other group members, so you can easily find each other if needed.
Of course, location sharing only works when a network connection is available. However, you can disable your network during your activity and only turn it on when necessary.
A group is automatically deleted if it is more than one week old.

Thank you for contributing to the Trailence community!
You’re about to publish your trail, which will make it visible to all users. Here’s some important information about how publishing works:

The published trail is a copy of your original trail. This means any changes you make to the trail you’re about to publish will not affect your original, private trail. Likewise, if you later modify your original trail, it won’t affect the published version.
At first, the trail will be saved as a “Draft”. This lets you prepare it for publication and make any adjustments you’d like compared to your original trail.
During this phase, you’ll be guided by a checklist to help you review key points before publishing. Among them:
Any offensive, abusive, or discriminatory content is strictly forbidden.
Remove any personal information you don’t wish to make public.
Do not include photos where people are recognizable.
Once your draft is ready, you can submit it for review. A moderator may then check it to ensure the rules are respected.
After validation, your track will be visible to the entire community!
You’ll still be able to edit or remove your published track at any time if you wish.
Thank you for your participation — and happy publishing!

The trail will be copied to your drafts. Editing works just like for a first publication: once your changes are made, they will be reviewed by a moderator. Do you confirm you want to edit this publication?

The name should be short and clearly describe the goal of the track. Here are a few examples:
Emerald Lake and Yoho Valley: clear and to the point.
Mount Hood via Timberline Trail: indicates both the destination and the chosen route if there are several options.
From Bondi to Coogee via the Coastal Walk: describes the starting point, destination, and route if relevant.
The description should help users quickly understand what to expect along the trail. Consider including:
Any potential difficulties (type and where they occur)
Viewpoints, points of interest, or notable features
The type of path (trail, wide track, road…) and an idea of the proportions if necessary
Whether the trail is mostly in forest, open terrain, or at altitude…
Any advice on the best time of year to hike it
If the trail is varied, a description of the main stages (e.g. forest at the start, chapel halfway, panoramic ridge at the end…)
Finish with practical information if relevant: parking availability, water points, etc.
Choose the primary activity for this route. It helps other users better understand its duration and identify routes that are suitable and actually accessible for that activity.
If possible, try to improve the quality of your track:
Fix any elevation values that seem incorrect.
If you left the main route (for a short technical break 🤭 for example), try to remove those sections from the track.
👉 To do this, use the Edit button on the map.
Consider adding waypoints to your trail:
They can be used to mark specific spots: a viewpoint, a landmark, a water source…
Most importantly, they help give directions, especially at places where the route isn’t obvious on site (like at a crossroads, or if the trail is poorly marked).
👉 To do this, use the Edit button on the map, select the desired location, and open the Waypoint menu.
Consider adding photos that make people want to follow your trail: beautiful landscapes, scenic viewpoints, unusual spots…
📍 Check that each photo is correctly positioned on the trail if this wasn’t done automatically.
⚠️ Do not publish photos where people are recognizable.
🙏 Also avoid sharing photos of private property without permission.

The purpose of smoothing is to remove GPS inaccuracies.
Because of these inaccuracies, it often happens that over a few meters the altitude goes up and down by a few meters, whereas in reality the slope is continuous.
Smoothing therefore works as follows:
  • We look for sections where the altitude varied within the configured threshold, over a configured maximum distance.
  • For each section found, we take the start altitude and the end altitude, and smooth it into a continuous slope.
  • To avoid losing the high or low points of the trail, if we find such a point in the middle of a section, we reduce the section to keep that point.

The original track is the raw track, exactly as recorded by the GPS or imported from a file.

When you edit the track, the original version is always preserved, allowing you to revert to it at any time — it serves as the reference track.

Even if you haven’t manually edited the track, Trailence automatically applies improvements to correct GPS inaccuracies.
We match the track to the Open Street Map paths

The estimated duration is calculated based on a base speed on flat terrain, then adjusted according to elevation gain, total duration, and taking into account short regular breaks (about 2–3 minutes every hour).

By default, the base speed is set to 5 km/h, which corresponds to the average speed of a hiker. You can change this value in your preferences.

The break time corresponds to the total duration of long breaks. This time is subtracted from the trail duration.

We distinguish between short breaks (to refresh yourself, enjoy the view, etc.) and long breaks (such as a picnic).

Short breaks are included in the displayed trail duration, as it’s normal to have brief pauses. However, when a long break is detected, its duration is deducted from the trail time, so the time shown doesn’t depend on how long you napped 😉. The deducted time appears in the Breaks section.

Long breaks are those lasting at least {{1}} minutes. This threshold can be configured in your preferences.
